facts.says: Osman is the Emir's spymaster and spends his days standing just outside Al Kharid palace.
Ask Osman who he is and he says only that he works for the Emir, and that you need know nothing more.
Nosy strangers don't trouble Osman; he reckons the city's secrets look after themselves.
Osman got all the adventuring he ever wanted out of his system when he was young, and is happy to stay put in Al Kharid now.
Osman points out that the desert has no single ruler: it's a scatter of independent city states and lawless bands, at peace for now but with old rivalries between some of them.
Al Kharid fought the Menaphites for a long time, and Osman holds that no war is ever really finished.
Osman is sure the Menaphites would know Al Kharid's spymaster on sight, and would lynch him if they caught him.
Osman thinks Chancellor Hassan is far too ready to trust outsiders when the palace ought to be careful.
Osman would rather a job were done quietly, with no needless risks and as little blood spilt as can be managed.
Leela, Osman's daughter, is one of his spies.
Osman's spies found that Prince Ali is held by bandits under the self-styled Lady Keli, in an old jail east of Draynor Village, with Leela keeping watch nearby.
Osman's plan is to deal with Keli, dress the prince up as her to get him past her men, and copy her cell key from a clay imprint and a bronze bar.
Since Prince Ali came home safe, Osman has kept the rescuer in mind for any dangerous job that comes up.
Osman adores sq'irk juice, which he swears makes a thief's fingers lighter and feet quicker, and he insists his self-control is excellent.
The sorceress who grows sq'irks near the south-east edge of Al Kharid was once Osman's friend, but they fell out and she gives him no more fruit.
Osman admits that Menaphos being shut tight to everyone is partly his own doing.
Kaleef, one of Osman's agents, was killed by a giant scarab in the tunnels beneath Sophanem, though he wounded it with his dagger first.
Keris daggers are standard kit for Osman's people, enchanted to work well against scarabs and kalphites, and he sells spares.
When the giant scarab attacked under Sophanem, Osman slipped into the shadows instead of fighting, and maintains he had it all under control.
After the business under Sophanem, Osman doesn't expect to go back down there any time soon, and won't say what he plans for Menaphos.
Ali Morrisane keeps a market stall in the north-east of Al Kharid, not far from the cactus patch.
Ali Morrisane calls himself the greatest salesman in the world.
Ali Morrisane was born in Pollnivneach, south across the sands, before setting up in Al Kharid.
Ali sells general goods, papyrus and desert robes from his stall, but never buys anything back.
Talk to Ali with a full purse and he'll manage to sell you some junk whether you wanted it or not: a raw chicken, a tinderbox, a bucket, a knife or a bronze pickaxe.
Ali complains he could sell far more with more staff, and would get on with selling sand to the Bedabin and trinkets to everyone else.
Ali admits a shopkeeper's life has no dragon slaying or damsel wooing in it, but says it has its own charms.
Ali's nephew in Pollnivneach was meant to come up and be his assistant, but hasn't turned up, and Ali offers a month of the lad's wages to whoever fetches him.
Ali sold the adventurer looking for his nephew a fake beard and a headdress for the trip to Pollnivneach.
Ali's nephew, young Baba, turned out to be such a good salesman that Pollnivneach called him a thief and he went into hiding, and Ali is terribly proud of him.
The whole hunt for Ali's nephew was really a tourism scheme: Ali was in league with Pollnivneach's camel seller, kebab seller and mayor.
Even after the business in Pollnivneach, Ali still has no assistant.
Ali Morrisane's flying carpet fleet is his own idea: he hired rug merchants to run carpet stations between the desert's busier places.
The carpets are enchanted rugs woven from ugthanki hair, and Ali won't sell a single one, since that would end his monopoly.
The gnomes of Gnome Air are unhappy about Ali's carpet network, and the glider captain in Al Kharid jokes it will never take off.
Ali's son Farid trades at the Grand Exchange, sent there by his father to spread the family business.
Once the Pollnivneach affair was done, Ali set about expanding, hunting for suppliers of runes, fine clothes and blackjacks.
Hassan is Chancellor to the Emir of Al Kharid, and works in the southern room of the palace's ground floor.
The Emir keeps to his private rooms these days, so Hassan does most of the actual running of Al Kharid.
Hassan is the money mind behind Al Kharid's prosperity and likes to keep a close eye on everything going on in the palace.
Hassan copes with the heat by reminding people that Al Kharid is rich and has water, and he hands out jugs of it to visitors who complain.
Hassan takes any talk of killing the palace's warriors as a poor joke.
Hassan won't have anyone treating the Emir's palace as a climbing frame by clambering in through its big window.
Hassan relies on Osman, the spymaster who stands just outside the palace, and sends would-be helpers to him.
The palace has an urgent problem: Prince Ali, the Emir's son and heir, has been taken, and Hassan is looking for someone who can get a job done.
Hassan has a reward ready, on the Emir's behalf, for whoever brings Prince Ali home.
Prince Ali is home safe, and the Emir is forever grateful to the one who rescued his son.
The Emir is too old and frail to thank the prince's rescuer in person, and spends most of his time resting.
Hassan counts the prince's rescuer a friend of Al Kharid, always welcome in the city, though still not trusted enough to climb in through the palace windows.
When Taiman's fishing crew washed up outside Al Kharid after meeting Tempoross, Hassan called the local seafarers together, and the Spirit Anglers were formed.
The Emir bought the old duelling arena north-east of the city and paid to have it done up as the Emir's Arena.
Shantay runs the pass between Al Kharid and the open desert, guarding it with his men and keeping it open and in repair.
Shantay's men keep outlaws from getting out of the desert and keep the inexperienced from dying of thirst in it.
Shantay sells passes for a small toll of five gold, and is offended at any hint he profits from it: it only covers repairs and his men's wages.
Shantay asks every newcomer to read the billboard poster at the pass, which lists the dangers of the desert.
Shantay recommends a full waterskin and a knife for the desert, since a knife will get juice out of a cactus.
Shantay warns that anyone walking into the desert in armour will bake, and sells desert clothes to keep travellers cool.
Shantay's shop sells waterskins, desert robes, shirts and boots, knives, rope, feathers, bronze bars, hammers and containers of water.
There's a chest at the pass where travellers can leave their things, and Shantay's people carry them to the bank.
Anyone who declares themselves an outlaw at the pass is thrown in Shantay's cell until they pay a small fine, or is shipped off to the prison in Port Sarim.
Shantay is put out when someone he jailed turns up free again, though he assumes the Port Sarim authorities know their business.
The guards at the desert gate send anyone without a pass back to Shantay, who they say charges a very reasonable price.
South of the pass the desert heat wears travellers down, faster in armour, and dries up the water in their jugs and bowls.
There are other Shantay passes further south at the Ruins of Unkah, kept by Shantay Guards.
Just past the gates sits Irena, a heartbroken mother whose daughter Ana went into the desert days ago and hasn't come back.
Irena has told Shantay that someone is out looking for her daughter Ana, which he thinks very brave.
Ana is safely back with her mother Irena, who expects the girl will be off on another trip before long.
